request.title: Why a positive screen is not a diagnosis
request.topic: Write a roughly 3-minute lesson in exactly 3 scenes for adults who know percentages but not conditional probability. Explain why a positive test need not mean the condition is likely. Use a hypothetical population of 1,000: 10 have the condition; the test is positive for 9 of them and for 99 of the 990 without it. Derive the positive-test probability of actually having the condition, then explain how changing prevalence while keeping sensitivity and false-positive rate fixed changes the result. Include one brief thinking pause. This is a toy probability example, not medical guidance.

draft.markdown:
# Why a positive screen is not a diagnosis

## Beat 1 — Follow a thousand people

Content needed: Hypothetical cohort of 1,000: 10 with the condition, 990 without. The test is positive for 9 of the 10 and 99 of the 990. Show all four outcomes, including 1 negative with the condition and 891 negatives without it. Use count-proportional areas, with enlarged detail explicitly marked. Preserve condition status when adding positive-result outlines. Do not show the combined positive count or posterior fraction yet.

Narration: Imagine a screening test comes back positive. How much does that tell us? We need more than a description of how well the test works. We also need to know how common the condition was before testing.

Narration: Here is a made-up population of one thousand people. Ten have the condition, and nine hundred ninety do not. This is a toy probability example, not medical guidance.

Narration: Among the ten with the condition, nine test positive and one tests negative. Among the nine hundred ninety without it, ninety-nine test positive and eight hundred ninety-one test negative.

Narration: The test catches nine out of ten people who have the condition. That sounds reassuring. But a positive result can come from either group. We need to follow both routes.

## Beat 2 — Change the group you count

Content needed: Keep the four outcome groups from beat-1. Isolate the 9 true positives and 99 false positives while keeping status colors. Show 108 total positives only when narration combines them. During the thinking pause, show the two counts and total but withhold the fraction's value and percentage. At the reveal, show 9/108 = 1/12 ≈ 8.3%. Distinguish P(positive | condition) from P(condition | positive) using plain-language set labels before any notation.

Narration: Now suppose all we know about one person is that their test was positive. Which group should we count? Only people with positive results. The negative results no longer belong in our comparison.

Narration: Nine people with the condition tested positive. So did ninety-nine people without it. Together, that makes one hundred eight positive results.

Invitation (spoken): Of these one hundred eight people, only nine have the condition. About what fraction is that? Take a few seconds to think.

Pause: 5s

Reveal (spoken): Nine out of one hundred eight is one in twelve, or about eight point three percent.

Narration: The ninety percent we started with answers a different question: among people with the condition, how many test positive? We just answered: among people who test positive, how many have the condition?

Narration: The test result raises the chance from one percent to about eight percent. It provides evidence, but in this population the condition is still unlikely.

## Beat 3 — Keep the test, change the population

Content needed: Preserve the positive-result comparison. Introduce a second hypothetical population of 1,000 with 100 having the condition and 900 without it. Hold sensitivity at 90% and false-positive rate at 10%. Derive 90 true positives and 90 false positives, then 90/180 = 50%. Compare with the original 9 versus 99 and 8.3% result. Counts or area lengths must share a stated linear scale within each comparison; do not suggest the same individuals acquire the condition. Finish with the two positive groups and the rate invariants, without a clinical recommendation.

Narration: What if the condition is more common? Keep the test exactly the same: ninety percent of people with the condition test positive, and ten percent of people without it test positive.

Narration: Consider a different population of one thousand, with one hundred who have the condition and nine hundred who do not. Now ninety people with the condition test positive. Ten percent of the other nine hundred gives ninety positive results without the condition.

Narration: That is ninety people with the condition among one hundred eighty positive results: fifty percent. The test's two rates stayed fixed, but the meaning of a positive changed.

Narration: Why? A more common condition supplies more true positives, while the smaller group without it supplies fewer false positives. When the condition is rare, even a modest false-positive rate can produce many more false positives than true ones.

Narration: To interpret a positive result, count both ways it could occur, then ask what share came from people with the condition. The starting prevalence is part of that answer.

# Why a positive screen is not a diagnosis

## Beat 1 — Two routes to a positive

Content needed: A hypothetical population of 1,000, represented by two bars on a common count scale: 10 with the condition in BLUE, 990 without it in GREY. State membership before showing results. Within those same bars, outline positive portions in YELLOW: 9 of 10 and 99 of 990. Keep membership colors visible. Label negative remainders 1 and 891 only if needed for the partition; do not display the final fraction yet. This is an exact toy population, not medical evidence.

Narration: Imagine a thousand people taking a screening test. Ten have a condition, and nine hundred ninety do not. This is a toy probability example, not medical guidance.

Narration: The test is positive for nine of the ten people with the condition. It catches ninety percent of that group. But it also gives a positive result to ninety-nine people without the condition: ten percent of that much larger group.

Narration: Those are two routes to the same positive result. A positive can come from someone with the condition, or from someone without it. To interpret a positive, we need to compare both routes.

## Beat 2 — Change the group we are counting

Content needed: Carry the same population bars. Extract their positive portions, retaining BLUE or GREY membership and YELLOW result outlines. Build one count-scaled positive bar from the two pieces: 9 with the condition, 99 without. The extraction filters by result; it does not change anyone's condition. Until Reveal, show those counts but hide 108, the quotient, percentages, and answer highlights. During Pause, freeze the evidence without new cues. At Reveal show 9 + 99 = 108, then 9/108 ≈ 8.3%.

Narration: Suppose all we know about a person is that their result is positive. We now restrict our attention to the positive group. The negative results leave our count, while the nine and the ninety-nine remain.

Invitation (spoken): Among these positives, roughly what fraction have the condition? Take five seconds to compare the two counts.

Pause: 5s

Reveal (spoken): There are a hundred eight positives altogether. Nine have the condition. Nine divided by a hundred eight is one in twelve, or about eight point three percent.

Narration: The ninety percent we started with answered a different question: among people with the condition, how many test positive? We are asking: among people testing positive, how many have the condition? The starting group changes, so the denominator changes.

## Beat 3 — Keep the test, change the population

Content needed: Retain the positive bar and its 9/108 result as a reference. Introduce a clearly distinct comparison population of 1,000 with 100 having the condition and 900 without. Use the same count scale and membership colors. Fix sensitivity at 90% and false-positive rate at 10%. Derive 90 true positives and 90 false positives, then their combined bar and 90/180 = 50%. The original people do not change membership; these are two hypothetical populations. Conclude with both positive bars compared on the common scale.

Narration: Now consider a different population of a thousand, with a hundred people who have the condition. Prevalence, the share who have it, has risen from one percent to ten percent.

Narration: Keep the test's two rates fixed. It still catches ninety percent of those with the condition, called its sensitivity. That now gives ninety positives. Its false-positive rate stays at ten percent. Among the nine hundred without the condition, that gives another ninety positives.

Narration: Now half the positives have the condition: ninety out of a hundred eighty. The test's rates stayed the same, but the balance between the two routes changed.

Narration: Higher prevalence supplies more true positives and fewer false positives in a population of fixed size. Lower prevalence does the reverse. A positive result becomes informative only when we combine how the test behaves with how common the condition was in the population being tested.

# Why a positive screen is not a diagnosis

## Beat 1 — Two ways to test positive

Content needed: A hypothetical population of 1,000, partitioned into 10 with the condition and 990 without it. Of these groups, respectively 9 and 99 test positive. Preserve condition membership when marking test results. Show 9/10 = 90% and 99/990 = 10% only alongside their spoken explanations. Do not yet show the combined positive total or the answer.

Narration: A test detects ninety percent of people who have a condition. If your result is positive, does that mean you have a ninety percent chance?

Narration: Let's count people in a toy example, not a medical recommendation. Among a thousand people, ten have the condition and nine hundred ninety do not. The test is positive for nine of those ten. That ninety percent detection rate is called sensitivity.

Narration: But it also gives a positive result to ninety-nine people without the condition. Ninety-nine out of nine hundred ninety is ten percent: the false-positive rate. So a positive result can come from either group. The test catches most people with the condition, but the group without it is much larger.

## Beat 2 — Change the group we count

Content needed: Retain the same people and result marks. Gather the 9 positives with the condition and 99 positives without it into one positive-only group. Reveal its total of 108 as narrated. During the thinking pause retain the two counts and total, but withhold the fraction and probability. At Reveal show 9/(9+99) = 9/108 = 1/12, approximately 8.3%.

Narration: Our question starts with a positive result, so we must now look only at people who tested positive. Bring together the nine who have the condition and the ninety-nine who do not. That makes a hundred eight positive results.

Invitation (spoken): Of those hundred eight people, what fraction actually have the condition? Take a moment to choose the numerator and denominator.

Pause: 6s

Reveal (spoken): Nine out of a hundred eight: one in twelve, or about eight point three percent. We divide by all positive results because that is the group we know we belong to. Ninety percent answered a different question: among people with the condition, how many test positive? Reversing the question changes which group goes underneath the fraction.

## Beat 3 — Same test, different population

Content needed: Keep the first result as a compact comparison, then explicitly introduce a different hypothetical population of 1,000 with 100 having the condition and 900 without it. Keep sensitivity 90% and false-positive rate 10% fixed. Show 90 true positives and 90 false positives, then 90/(90+90) = 50%. Compare prevalence 1% versus 10%, and resulting probabilities approximately 8.3% versus 50%.

Narration: Now imagine a different thousand people: a hundred have the condition, and nine hundred do not. The condition's prevalence, its share of the population, has risen from one percent to ten percent. Keep the test's two rates unchanged.

Narration: Ninety percent of a hundred gives ninety positive results from people with the condition. Ten percent of nine hundred gives ninety from people without it. Now half of the hundred eighty positive results come from people with the condition.

Narration: The test has not improved. The mixture entering it has changed. Higher prevalence supplies more true positives and fewer false positives; lower prevalence does the reverse, with these rates fixed. To interpret a positive result in this model, count both routes to positive, then ask what share came from the condition. A positive result alone does not tell you that share.
